people.name: Sossina M. Haile
body: Sossina Haile's family left Ethiopia after the 1974 revolution. In her own words, "soldiers came to our house to try and arrest my father," a historian, and the family "were lucky enough to be able to flee the country." She grew up in the United States and finished high school in Minnesota at Saint John's Preparatory School in Collegeville, which lists her among its notable alumni, class of 1983.

She earned a B.S. in materials science and engineering at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, an M.S. at the University of California, Berkeley, and a Ph.D. back at MIT in 1992. She then spent two years at the Max Planck Institute for Solid State Research in Stuttgart, Germany, as a Fulbright and then a Humboldt fellow. Materials science asks how the arrangement of atoms in a solid determines what it can do. Haile focused on solids that conduct ions, the charged particles that move inside batteries and fuel cells.

She spent 18 years on the faculty of the California Institute of Technology and became known for her work on solid acid fuel cells, devices that turn chemical fuel into electricity using a class of proton-conducting solids. In 2010 the American Institute of Chemists gave her its Chemical Pioneer Award for establishing new classes of fuel cells. Newsweek named her one of twelve people to watch in 2008, and in 2012 she received the International Ceramics Prize from the World Academy of Ceramics.

In 2015 she moved to Northwestern University, where she is the Walter P. Murphy Professor of Materials Science and Engineering. Her lab works on materials for sustainable energy, including protonic ceramic fuel cells that can run directly on ammonia. She is a fellow of the Ethiopian Academy of Sciences and a board member of Ethiopia Education Initiatives.
keyFacts: Family fled Ethiopia after the 1974 revolution.
1983: Graduated from Saint John's Preparatory School, Collegeville, Minnesota.
1992: Ph.D., MIT, after a B.S. at MIT and an M.S. at UC Berkeley.
18 years on the Caltech faculty; known for work on solid acid fuel cells.
2010: Chemical Pioneer Award, American Institute of Chemists.
2012: International Ceramics Prize, World Academy of Ceramics.
2015: Moved to Northwestern University.
people.connectToWork: When a person's family left a country because of political danger, how would you make room for that history in your work without asking them to retell it?

people.name: Zinet Kemal
body: On January 2, 2013, Zinet Kemal landed at Minneapolis–Saint Paul International Airport with her husband and their three-year-old child. She was seven months pregnant, and in Ethiopia she had studied law. The family had come through the U.S. Diversity Immigrant Visa program, often called the visa lottery, which admits a limited number of people each year from countries with low rates of U.S. immigration.

Kemal was born and raised in Addis Ababa and lived in Harar in eastern Ethiopia at ages eight and nine, while her mother looked for work. She studied law at Jimma University. In Minnesota she started over, beginning at Saint Paul College and earning a bachelor's degree in computer science from Metropolitan State University in 2018. She started as an intern at Hennepin County, which became a full-time auditor job, then worked in Minnesota state government and at Best Buy, and earned a master's degree in cybersecurity from Georgia Tech. As of a July 2026 Saint Paul College profile she is a senior cloud security engineer at Mayo Clinic.

She began writing books for her own children. The first, Proud in Her Hijab (2021), is about a girl who wears a hijab, a headscarf worn by some Muslim women and girls. It won a 2021 Distinguished Authors Guild Award in the children's category. Oh, No… Hacked Again! explains online safety to children, and Saint Paul College says she has since written four more books on online safety, cybersecurity careers and digital citizenship. She also gave a TEDxMinneapolis talk on keeping children safe online.

Ethiopia's people include Muslims as well as Christians, and Harar is one of the oldest centers of Islam in the Horn of Africa. By Sahan Journal's 2021 account, Kemal lives in Blaine with her husband and four children.
keyFacts: Studied law at Jimma University, Ethiopia.
January 2013: Arrived in Minnesota through the Diversity Visa program.
2018: B.S. in computer science, Metropolitan State University.
2021: Published Proud in Her Hijab.
Master's degree in cybersecurity, Georgia Tech.
As of July 2026: Senior cloud security engineer, Mayo Clinic.
people.connectToWork: When a person's credentials or experience come from another country, what does your process do with them? What would you ask before starting them over at the beginning?

people.name: Kamal Mohamed
body: Kamal Mohamed's business education started at his family's food truck. He was 10 when his family moved from Ethiopia to a high-rise apartment in Minneapolis's Cedar Riverside neighborhood. As a teenager he sold root-beer floats at high school sporting events, netting $60, a moment he calls his first entrepreneurial "aha." In college he earned tips serving snacks after bar time.

Shortly after college, in 2011, he co-founded a Minneapolis food truck festival. Racket calls it the MN Food Truck Fair and Sahan Journal calls it the Uptown Food Truck Festival. The first year brought operational chaos and complaints about long lines. In the second year, attendance quintupled. He ran it for three years before selling it, and went on to run the Minnesota Food Truck business. With his brother Arif he started Nashville Coop, a hot chicken food truck that grew into three brick-and-mortar locations, and in Northeast Minneapolis he opened StepChld, a restaurant serving Ethiopian-inspired food.

In 2024 he opened the first Parcelle, a clean-eating café in Northeast Minneapolis known for smoothies and high-protein breakfast burritos. Artful Living reported plans for further locations in 2026 in downtown Minneapolis, the North Loop and Wayzata. He also co-founded Gallant Tiger, a premium sandwich company. In 2026 the Minneapolis St. Paul Business Journal named him to its 40 Under 40 list. Accepting the honor, he said that when someone in the Twin Cities has an idea or a dream, "people will move out of the way and help you get there."
keyFacts: Moved from Ethiopia to Minneapolis with his family at age 10.
2011: Co-founded a Minneapolis food truck festival; ran it three years, then sold it.
Co-founder of Nashville Coop; founder of StepChld.
2024: Opened Parcelle in Northeast Minneapolis.
Co-founder of Gallant Tiger, a sandwich company.
2026: Minneapolis St. Paul Business Journal 40 Under 40 honoree.

people.name: Dinaw Mengestu
body: Dinaw Mengestu was born in Addis Ababa in 1978. By the account of the Berlin International Literature Festival and public radio station WYPR, his father had fled Ethiopia during the political repression known as the Red Terror. His father went to the United States, and in 1980, when Dinaw was about two, the rest of the family followed.

The family settled first in Peoria, Illinois, then the Chicago area, where Mengestu graduated from Fenwick High School in Oak Park. He earned a B.A. from Georgetown University in 2000 and an M.F.A. from Columbia University in 2005. His first novel, The Beautiful Things That Heaven Bears (2007), follows an Ethiopian immigrant who runs a struggling corner store in Washington, D.C. It won the Guardian First Book Award and a Los Angeles Times Book Prize, and in 2007 the National Book Foundation named him one of its "5 Under 35."

His second novel, How to Read the Air (2010), follows an Ethiopian American son retracing his parents' troubled marriage, and in 2010 The New Yorker placed him on its "20 Under 40" list. In 2012 he received a MacArthur Fellowship; the foundation highlighted his fiction about African immigrants whose memories are shaped by violence in their home countries. He followed with All Our Names (2014) and Someone Like Us (2024). He directs the Written Arts program at Bard College.
keyFacts: 1978: Born in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.
1980: Family joined his father in the United States; raised in Peoria and the Chicago area.
2000: B.A., Georgetown University; 2005: M.F.A., Columbia University.
2007: The Beautiful Things That Heaven Bears; Guardian First Book Award; "5 Under 35."
2010: How to Read the Air; New Yorker "20 Under 40."
2012: MacArthur Fellow.
2014 and 2024: All Our Names and Someone Like Us.
people.connectToWork: Parents and children in one family may remember a country very differently. How would you ask each of them what they want you to know, rather than letting one speak for the other?

people.name: Julie Mehretu
body: Around 1977, during the Derg's Red Terror, the family of a young girl named Julie Mehretu fled Addis Ababa for East Lansing, Michigan, where both parents resumed teaching: her father, Assefa Mehretu, an Ethiopian professor of geography offered a job at Michigan State University, and her mother, Doree Mehretu, an American Montessori teacher. Mehretu was born in Addis Ababa on November 28, 1970.

She spent 1990–91 at Cheikh Anta Diop University in Dakar, Senegal, earned a B.A. from Kalamazoo College in 1992, and earned an M.F.A. from the Rhode Island School of Design in 1997. She became known for enormous paintings that begin with architectural drawings, maps and plans of public spaces such as museums, stadiums and airports, then layer them with bursts of abstract marks and color. The MacArthur Foundation, which named her a Fellow in 2005, described one early work, Transcending: The New International (2003), as mapping the buildings and urban plans of African capital cities onto a single landscape, overlaid with lines that trace migrations and battlefronts.

Her large commissions include Mural, a 90-foot painting commissioned by Goldman Sachs in 2007 for the lobby of its Manhattan headquarters, and Uprising of the Sun, an 83-by-25-foot work for the north facade of the Barack Obama Presidential Center's museum building, announced in September 2024. She received the U.S. Department of State Medal of Arts from Secretary of State John Kerry in 2015 and was named to Time's list of the 100 most influential people in 2020. She lives and works in New York City.

About 1977: Family moved to East Lansing, Michigan.
1997: M.F.A., Rhode Island School of Design.
2005: MacArthur Fellow.
2015: U.S. Department of State Medal of Arts.
2020: Time 100 Most Influential People.
people.connectToWork: Does your form let a person name more than one heritage, or does it make them choose? What would you do with the answer?

people.name: Marcus Samuelsson
body: In 1991 a young cook trained in Gothenburg, Sweden, arrived in New York City as an apprentice at Aquavit, an upscale Swedish restaurant. At 24 he became its executive chef, and he soon became the youngest chef to receive a three-star review from The New York Times. The chef was Marcus Samuelsson, and his story began in Ethiopia.

Samuelsson was born on November 6, 1970, in Ethiopia as Kassahun Tsegie. By Britannica's account, he and his older sister, Fantaye, lost their mother to tuberculosis when they were young; the Carnegie Corporation's Great Immigrants profile says both his biological parents died in a tuberculosis epidemic. In 1973 Lennart and Ann Marie Samuelsson, a couple from Gothenburg, adopted the two children, who were renamed Marcus and Linda. He grew up in Gothenburg and trained at the city's culinary institute before working in kitchens abroad.

He became a U.S. citizen in 2000. The James Beard Foundation named him its Rising Star Chef in 1999 and Best Chef: New York City in 2003. In 2010 he opened Red Rooster in Harlem, a restaurant built around American comfort food and the culture and history of the neighborhood. The same year he was named a Carnegie Great Immigrant. In 2012 he published a memoir, Yes, Chef, written with Veronica Chambers.

His life is a reminder that Ethiopian-born people have reached other countries in different ways: as political refugees, as students, through the visa lottery and, as in his case, as adopted children raised elsewhere.
keyFacts: November 6, 1970: Born in Ethiopia as Kassahun Tsegie.
1973: Adopted with his sister by Lennart and Ann Marie Samuelsson; raised in Gothenburg.
1991: Came to New York as an apprentice at Aquavit; executive chef at 24.
1999 and 2003: James Beard Rising Star Chef and Best Chef: New York City.
2010: Opened Red Rooster in Harlem; named a Carnegie Great Immigrant.
2012: Memoir Yes, Chef published.
people.connectToWork: What might you assume about a person's language, faith or sense of home from their birthplace or their name? How would you ask instead?

people.name: Maaza Mengiste
body: On September 15, 2020, the Booker Prize, one of the most prestigious awards for fiction in English, announced its six-novel shortlist. One was The Shadow King, by the Ethiopian-born American writer Maaza Mengiste. Its subject was Mussolini's invasion of Ethiopia in 1935, told through the women who fought it.

Mengiste was born in Addis Ababa and lived in Nigeria and Kenya before settling in the United States. She earned a B.A. at the University of Michigan in 1993 and an M.F.A. in creative writing at New York University in 2007, and has held a Fulbright scholarship and fellowships from the National Endowment for the Arts and Creative Capital.

Her first novel, Beneath the Lion's Gaze (2010), is set in Addis Ababa during the revolution and the political violence that followed. The Shadow King (2019) reaches further back: a woman helps disguise a peasant as the emperor and becomes his guard, inspiring other women to take up arms. She also edited the anthology Addis Ababa Noir (2020).

Italy occupied Ethiopia from 1936 to 1941. Mengiste's books bring that history to a wide English-speaking audience while centering women left out of official accounts. She is a professor of English at Wesleyan University, after earlier posts at Princeton University and Queens College, and in 2026 she was named a MacArthur Fellow.
keyFacts: Born in Addis Ababa; lived in Nigeria and Kenya before settling in the United States.
B.A., University of Michigan (1993); M.F.A., New York University (2007); Fulbright scholar.

people.name: Zeresenay Alemseged
body: In 2000, at Dikika in Ethiopia's Afar region, a team led by the Ethiopian scientist Zeresenay "Zeray" Alemseged found a fossil embedded in sandstone. Years of careful work revealed the nearly complete skeleton of a child about two and a half years old who lived about 3.3 million years ago. The child belonged to Australopithecus afarensis, the same species as the famous "Lucy," and became known as Selam.

Alemseged, who was born in Axum in northern Ethiopia, earned a B.Sc. in geology at Addis Ababa University (1990), an M.Sc. in paleontology at the University of Montpellier II (1994) and a Ph.D. in paleoanthropology at the University of Paris VI and the National Museum of Natural History in Paris (1998). He leads the Dikika Research Project. When he and colleagues presented Selam in the journal Nature in 2006, he was at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig, Germany. About two years later he moved to the California Academy of Sciences in San Francisco. In fall 2016 he joined the University of Chicago as the Donald N. Pritzker Professor of Organismal Biology and Anatomy, and in 2021 he was elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences.

A 2017 study he co-authored found that spinal features that make efficient upright walking possible appeared millions of years earlier than once thought. Alemseged spends several months each year in the Afar region and works with the National Museum of Ethiopia, where fossils are prepared and curated. He told the University of Chicago, "one-half of my lab is back there."
keyFacts: Born in Axum, Ethiopia; leads the Dikika Research Project in the Afar region.
1990, 1994, 1998: B.Sc. (Addis Ababa), M.Sc. (Montpellier II), Ph.D. (Paris VI).
2000: His team found the Selam fossil, about 3.3 million years old, at Dikika.
2006: Selam presented in Nature.
2016: Joined the University of Chicago as Donald N. Pritzker Professor.
2021: Elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences.
people.connectToWork: If the materials your team uses show a country only through famine or conflict, what would you add, and who would you ask?

people.name: Kelela
body: Kelela Mizanekristos was born in Washington, D.C., in 1983 and grew up an only child in Gaithersburg, Maryland, the daughter of Ethiopian immigrants from the town of Bati who had come to the United States on scholarships in the 1970s. She played violin and sang in her school choir. She briefly studied sociology at American University before turning to music, singing jazz standards at open-mic nights in a Washington café in 2007. She later moved to Los Angeles.

Performing under her first name, she built a following with the mixtape Cut 4 Me (2013) and the six-track EP Hallucinogen (2015), blending R&B with electronic and club music. Her debut album, Take Me Apart (2017, Warp), drew wide critical acclaim. She returned with Raven (February 2023), followed by New Avatar (Warp, July 2026).

In a 2017 interview with Minnesota Public Radio's The Current, she described her Ethiopian heritage as a source of both pride and belonging, and at times of distance from some Black American peers, while identifying firmly as a Black woman: "I'm Black. I'm a Black woman."

2013 and 2015: Cut 4 Me (mixtape) and Hallucinogen (EP).
2017: Debut album Take Me Apart.
2023 and 2026: Albums Raven and New Avatar.

people.name: Alexander "Skunder" Boghossian
body: In 1965 New York's Museum of Modern Art bought a painting called Juju's Wedding (1964) by a young artist from Addis Ababa. By AllAfrica's and BlackPast's accounts, he was the first contemporary African artist whose work MoMA had purchased. Two years earlier the Musée d'Art Moderne in Paris had bought his work, the first time it did so for an Ethiopian painter. The painter was Alexander Boghossian, known as Skunder.

Skunder was born in Addis Ababa in 1937. At 17 he won an imperial scholarship to study at St. Martin's School of Art in London. He then moved to Paris, where he studied and taught at the Académie de la Grande Chaumière, and he returned to Ethiopia from 1966 to 1969.

He came to the United States around 1970 as artist in residence at Atlanta University and instructor at the Atlanta Center for Black Art, and he also taught at Hampton University. By the Smithsonian's account, the 1974 revolution kept him from going home, and he lived as a permanent resident and artist in exile. In 1974 he began teaching at Howard University in Washington, D.C., the historically Black university, where he taught for close to three decades.

The Smithsonian's National Museum of African Art owns his painting End of the Beginning (1972–73), and its exhibition Ethiopian Passages: Dialogues in the Diaspora opened in May 2003, just before his death in Washington that month. The artist Kebedech Tekleab called his death "a great loss."

1963: Paris's Musée d'Art Moderne buys his work.
1965: MoMA acquires Juju's Wedding (1964).

people.connectToWork: Someone may be unable to go home for political reasons, for decades. How could your process account for that when it asks about family, documents or plans?

people.name: Mulatu Astatke
body: In the 1960s a young musician from Jimma, in southwestern Ethiopia, enrolled at Berklee College of Music in Boston, where he studied vibraphone and percussion. Berklee calls him its first African graduate. His name was Mulatu Astatke, and the sound he went on to build has a name of its own: Ethio-jazz, a blend of Ethiopian music with jazz, Latin, funk and soul.

Mulatu was born on December 19, 1943. His family sent him to Britain in the 1950s to study engineering, but at Lindisfarne College in Wales and then Trinity College of Music in London he turned to music, before coming to Boston. In New York City he recorded the Latin-jazz-influenced Afro-Latin Soul albums in 1966 and later Mulatu of Ethiopia.

He returned to Addis Ababa in 1969, and much of his early-1970s work came out on Amha Records, a label that closed in 1975 under the Derg military government. In 1973 he played as a guest with Duke Ellington's orchestra on its tour of Ethiopia. After the Derg took power, he stayed in Ethiopia and taught music.

In the late 1990s the French Éthiopiques CD reissues brought his music to new listeners, and director Jim Jarmusch used his music in the 2005 film Broken Flowers. In 2007–2008 he was a fellow at Harvard's Radcliffe Institute. In 2012 Berklee gave him an honorary doctorate and he gave its commencement address. In 2025 Strut Records released Mulatu Plays Mulatu, and he announced his retirement from touring. National Geographic profiled him at 82 in January 2026, still performing and working on software to expand the notes available on traditional Ethiopian instruments.
keyFacts: December 19, 1943: Born in Jimma, Ethiopia.
1960s: Studies at Berklee College of Music, Boston.
1966: Records Afro-Latin Soul in New York City.
1973: Plays with Duke Ellington's orchestra on its Ethiopia tour.
2005: Music featured in Broken Flowers.

people.name: Sara Menker
people.field: Business, technology, agriculture and climate data
body: In 2021 Time magazine named Gro Intelligence, the company Sara Menker founded, one of its 100 most influential companies. She had left a Wall Street career to build a company that used data and computer models to forecast what happens to the world's food.

Menker grew up in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. As a child she lived through the effects of famine and political unrest: "Fuel was rationed, sugar was rationed," she told Columbia Magazine. "It didn't matter if you were rich or poor." She graduated from Mount Holyoke College in Massachusetts in 2004, majoring in economics, and later from Columbia Business School (class of 2012).

At Morgan Stanley she started in commodities risk management, moved into trading and became a vice president in the firm's commodities group. In 2008, during the financial crisis, she began researching farmland prices in Ethiopia, a personal interest that she says "grew into a complete obsession." In 2012 she founded Gro Intelligence, a data platform for global food and agricultural markets, and led it as CEO. The World Economic Forum named her a Young Global Leader, and her 2017 TED talk on a coming global food crisis has been viewed about 1.9 million times. Columbia Magazine reports that she was later included on Time's list of the 100 most influential people.
Gro Intelligence had a difficult end. She was replaced as CEO in February 2024, and at the end of May 2024 the company told staff it was shutting down.
keyFacts: Grew up in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.
2004: Graduated from Mount Holyoke College (economics).

2012: Founded Gro Intelligence; CEO until February 2024.
2017: TED talk, "A global food crisis may be less than a decade away."
2021: Gro Intelligence named to Time's 100 most influential companies.

people.connectToWork: When you ask about food or money, how would you ask in a way that leaves room for a person's past experience of scarcity, without assuming they have had it?

people.name: Mimi Alemayehou
body: From 2010 to 2014 Mimi Alemayehou was Executive Vice President of the Overseas Private Investment Corporation (OPIC), the U.S. government's development finance agency, which helps American companies invest in emerging markets. In that post she became one of the architects of Power Africa, President Barack Obama's effort to expand electricity access across the continent.

Alemayehou was born in Ethiopia and spent her early years in Kenya before emigrating to the United States, where she became a naturalized citizen. She earned a master's degree at the Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy at Tufts University and began her career working for U.S. Representative Mac Thornberry of Texas.

She managed a multi-country African trade project for the International Executive Service Corps, served as director of international regulatory affairs at WorldSpace, a satellite telecommunications company, and founded a consulting firm, Trade Links. President George W. Bush appointed her U.S. Executive Director on the board of the African Development Bank, where she pushed the bank to lend more to the private sector for infrastructure and to become more transparent. The Treasury Secretary gave her a Distinguished Honor Award for that service.

The Payne Institute reports that during her four years at OPIC its portfolio grew more than 24 percent to $18 billion and its Africa portfolio nearly tripled to almost $4 billion. After leaving government in 2014 she joined Black Rhino Group as managing director and became executive advisor and chair of Blackstone Africa Infrastructure.
keyFacts: Born in Ethiopia; early years in Kenya; naturalized U.S. citizen.

people.name: Senait Fisseha
body: When Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus became the first African to lead the World Health Organization, one of the people at his side was Senait Fisseha, the Ethiopian-born chair of his election campaign, a physician and attorney from the University of Michigan who went on to serve as chief advisor to the WHO Director-General.

Fisseha is an obstetrician-gynecologist who earned a joint J.D./M.D. at Southern Illinois University in 1999. She built her clinical and academic career at the University of Michigan, where she was medical director of the Center for Reproductive Medicine and chief of the reproductive endocrinology and infertility division. She was the founding executive director of the Center for International Reproductive Health Training (CIRHT), which works with medical schools abroad, including in Ethiopia, to train doctors and nurses in family planning and reproductive health.

As of August 2026 she is vice president of global programs at the Susan Thompson Buffett Foundation. She co-chaired the Conference on Public Health in Africa in 2023. By Southern Illinois University's account, she returned to Africa in 2020 and lives in Rwanda. On August 26, 2026, Africa CDC unveiled a statue in her honor at its Addis Ababa headquarters. Her honors include the Ethiopian Ministry of Health's highest award and a place on New African's 100 Most Influential Africans (2018).

Chair of Tedros's WHO campaign; later chief advisor to him at WHO.
Founding executive director of CIRHT at the University of Michigan.

people.name: Abebe Bikila
body: Abebe Bikila was born on August 7, 1932, in Jato, Ethiopia. He won the Olympic marathon in 1960 and again in 1964, the first person to win the event at consecutive Games.

In 1969 he was injured in a car crash. The Association of International Marathons (AIMS) dates it to the night of March 22 and says he was paralysed below the neck; Olympedia says late 1969. He was treated at Stoke Mandeville Hospital in England, for about eight months by AIMS's account, and regained use of his arms. He then took up wheelchair archery and, per AIMS, table tennis, and competed at the Stoke Mandeville Games, a forerunner of the Paralympics. Olympedia places his competition in 1969; AIMS places it in 1970.

He died in Addis Ababa on October 25, 1973, aged 41. AIMS gives the cause as a brain hemorrhage related to the accident. We found no account in his own words of what disability meant to him, so this page does not describe his views.
keyFacts: 1960 and 1964: Olympic marathon gold medals.
1969: Became disabled in a car crash.
Competed in wheelchair archery at the Stoke Mandeville Games.
1973: Died in Addis Ababa, aged 41.
people.connectToWork: When a person's disability came later in life, how would you ask what they want to keep doing and what has changed, rather than starting from what they have lost?

people.name: Tigist Gezahagn Menigstu
body: Tigist Gezahagn Menigstu is an Ethiopian Paralympic middle-distance runner who competes in the T13 classification, for athletes with low vision. Her name also appears as Mengistu. She won the women's 1500 m T13 at Tokyo 2020. The International Paralympic Committee calls it the first Paralympic gold medal for Ethiopia.

In May 2024 she won her first World Para Athletics Championships gold in Kobe, Japan, in a championship record of 4:18.90, which the committee says "continued her domination in the category." On August 31, 2024, she defended her Paralympic title in Paris in 4:22.39.

institutions.name: Little Ethiopia, Los Angeles
body: In 1988 Ethiopian immigrant Fekere Gebre-Mariam moved his restaurant, Rosalind's, to South Fairfax Avenue in Los Angeles, and it became an anchor for the block. By 1994 the block had five Ethiopian restaurants, a coffeehouse, a market, a travel agency and a silk-screen shop. People began calling it "Little Addis," after Ethiopia's capital.

The block had once been an extension of the Jewish commercial district of Fairfax to the north, and remnants of Hebrew survive on some signs. Business owners, including Birhanu and Getahun Asfaw of the restaurant Messob, lobbied the city to recognize the street. In November 2002 the Los Angeles City Council unanimously named it Little Ethiopia. The Los Angeles Almanac calls it the smallest of the city's 18 officially recognized ethnic enclaves and the only one honoring an African culture. PBS SoCal says the official street signs went up in 2004.
The district's first street festival drew about 5,000 people, and the Almanac says it has been held every September since.
keyFacts: 1988: Rosalind's moves to South Fairfax Avenue.
1994: Five Ethiopian restaurants on the block.

institutions.name: Ethiopian Community in Minnesota
body: The Ethiopian Community in Minnesota (ECM) is a St. Paul organization whose Amharic-language statement describes it as member-supported and open to all Ethiopians, regardless of religion, language, ethnicity or gender. Its website lists notary services, help with documents, referrals to agencies, references and representation for first-time renters, civic engagement and cultural activities, with office hours on Monday and Friday.

In a 2022 request to the Minnesota Legislature (HF 3908, with Senate companion SF 3886), ECM said it was working from an office of eight feet by ten feet. The request sought $2.5 million to buy and repair a building at 1630 University Avenue in St. Paul's Midway area. A survey of Ethiopians had picked the Midway because many people knew the area and it was easy to reach by public transportation. ECM described a center for teaching children languages and traditions, holidays, weddings and graduations, support for families in mourning, a library, translation of documents and school transcripts, job training, computer classes, counseling and support groups. A 2023 bill, HF 2707, sought $2.24 million. We found no record that either bill passed or that the building was bought, and as of October 2026 ECM still lists Rice Street.

The same request estimated that 45,000 to 50,000 people in and around the Twin Cities identify as Ethiopian or Ethiopian American. That is the organization's own estimate, not a count; the document does not state a date, and the 2022 date may come from the bill. Mpls.St.Paul Magazine said in 2021 that at least 30,000 Ethiopians, most of them Oromo, live in the state; it does not give a source for the count, and definitions vary. Mpls.St.Paul said in 2024 that nearly 40,000 live in the metro, and Chala, in MinnPost in June 2026, gives 35,000 to 50,000. An AP and MPR News report in 2019 gave about 100,000 with no source, so do not repeat that figure without that warning.
keyFacts: Based in St. Paul; said in 2022 that it worked from an 8-by-10-foot office.
2022: HF 3908 / SF 3886 requested $2.5 million for a community center.
2023: HF 2707 requested $2.24 million.
2022 own estimate: 45,000–50,000 people in and around the Twin Cities.

institutions.name: Ethiopian Fest of Minnesota
institutions.location: Twin Cities metro (St. Paul, Woodbury, Eden Prairie)
body: On Labor Day weekend in 2022, the organizer Ethiopian Day Fest held its fourth annual Ethiopian Fest of Minnesota at Aerie Stadium at Eden Prairie High School, after earlier editions in St. Paul and Woodbury. It billed the event as the state's largest family-friendly festival of Ethiopian culture.

The main day, September 4, featured Ethiopian businesses and restaurants, a traditional fashion show, soccer games and live music, with opening and closing concerts in West St. Paul. A participant, Henok Alemayehu Degfu, told the local paper that the event gathers Ethiopians of all backgrounds, and noted that Ethiopian New Year, on September 11, was coming soon.

We found no edition after 2022, and the festival's own website would not connect. In summer 2026 the large Ethiopian gathering in Minnesota was the Ethiopian Sports Federation in North America's tournament, listed below. Public New Year events continue: the Ethiopian Community in Minnesota invited people to a celebration at Highland Park Pavilion on Sept. 13, 2026.
keyFacts: About 2019: First festival, counting back from the fourth in 2022.
September 4, 2022: Fourth annual festival, Eden Prairie High School.
No edition found after 2022.

institutions.name: Ethiopian Center for Disability and Development
body: The Ethiopian Center for Disability and Development (ECDD) says its founders came together in 2005 to discuss how to get persons with disabilities better access to mainstream services and development programs. It was registered with Ethiopia's Ministry of Justice in December 2005. Its site names Bob Ransom and Yetnebersh Nigussie as co-founders, and AMECEA reported in 2015 that Yetnebersh Nigussie became its second Executive Director.

It works with other organizations to promote "disability inclusive development," meaning that people with disabilities are included in government and nongovernmental services and development programs. Its program areas are rights of persons with disabilities, inclusive health, inclusive education, inclusive livelihoods, social inclusion and protection, and inclusive humanitarian response. It also runs the Minch disability information platform, the Ethiopian Business and Disability Network and ECDD Academy.
keyFacts: December 2005: Registered with Ethiopia's Ministry of Justice.
Co-founders: Bob Ransom and Yetnebersh Nigussie.
Runs the Minch disability information platform and the Ethiopian Business and Disability Network.

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Here, Ethiopian means people of any of Ethiopia's many peoples, including Amhara, Oromo, Tigrayan, Somali, Gurage, Sidama, Wolaita and Anuak people, who speak many languages and follow Orthodox, Muslim, Protestant, Catholic and traditional faiths. We did not find a Minnesota-based study of how Ethiopian Minnesotans understand disability. The evidence below is mostly small studies and theses from different regions of Ethiopia, read as abstracts or summaries. Region, faith, generation, education and whether a family came from a city or a rural area can all make a large difference. The Amharic and Oromo pages in this collection add research this page does not repeat.
questions: Which language would you like to use, and which interpreter would you be comfortable with?
Is there anything about an interpreter's background that matters to you, such as privacy or where they are from?
What do you, and the people around you, call this? What words would you like me to use?
Has anyone given you a label or a diagnosis? Who gave it to you, and has it helped?
What do you want a label or assessment to open up for you? Is there anything you want it to avoid?
Who would you like included in decisions and meetings?
If you would like to share it, what have you been told about why this happened? What would be helpful to know?
Are there faith practices, holidays or fasting periods we should plan around?
How is caregiving affecting your work, money and health?
How do you prefer to get information: spoken, written in English, or written in your first language?
What would you like to know about what happens to your information and who sees it?

context.heading: What studies in Ethiopia have asked
body: In South Gondar in the Amhara region, a 2023 study surveyed 970 adults with disabilities and interviewed 16. It found that misconceptions about the causes of disability and assumptions about what disabled people can do worsen stigma and limit participation. The authors recommend challenging those norms through community-based inclusive development (Breffka and colleagues).

In Sebeta Hawass district in Oromia, a 2015 anthropology thesis used interviews, observation and focus groups. It found that local belief systems strongly shape how people there understand disability, that some religious acts and texts portray disabled people as cursed or sinful, and that disabled people face barriers to education, health care and information. It also looked at resilience through the lives of disabled people who have succeeded (Adugna Lema, abstract).

In Dilla Town in southern Ethiopia, a 2025 qualitative study of congenital anomalies reported that many respondents saw them as a curse, divine punishment or the result of parents' sins, and that some linked them to contraceptive pills, the mother's diet or magic. The authors tie this to limited information about medical causes. We read a summary, which gives no sample size (Getnet and colleagues).
None of these studies describes a Minnesota family, and none tells you what any one person thinks. Ask, and offer clear information in the person's own language without correcting their account.

context.heading: Caregivers
body: The Dilla summary reports social isolation, psychological distress and economic hardship for affected families. It is one study in one town. It is a reason to ask how a caregiver is doing and to connect them to caregiver supports, as well as to plan with the disabled person.

context.heading: Language, interpreters and fears about information
body: Do not assume an Ethiopian family speaks Amharic. Afaan Oromo, Tigrinya, Somali and others are all possible, and the choice of language or interpreter can carry ethnic or political meaning. Never use children as interpreters.

A spokesperson for the Ethiopian Sports Federation in North America told MPR News in June 2026 that federal immigration enforcement in Minnesota had frightened many community members. The Oromo Community of Minnesota posted a response in December 2025 to the revocation of Temporary Protected Status for Ethiopian nationals. Explain to every family what happens to personal information and that services are separate from immigration enforcement. Do not assume who has concerns.

context.heading: What we could not find
body: We found no study of Ethiopian families' understanding of disability in Minnesota, no documented disability terms in Ethiopian languages, no source on who makes decisions in Ethiopian families, and no research on Muslim, Protestant or traditional healing around disability among Ethiopians. We found no Minnesota organization specific to Ethiopian disability. The Ethiopian Community in Minnesota does not list disability services. Recent conflict in Ethiopia, including in Tigray and Oromia, may affect some newcomers, but we found no research on what it means for services, so ask rather than assume.
Faith practice and formal services can sit side by side. Ask what practices matter to the person, and involve a congregation or mosque only with their consent.

organizations.intro: MPR News described Ethiopians in Minnesota in 2005 as "a diverse group," and that group includes many peoples, languages and faiths. Teferi Fufa's MNopedia history traces Oromo organizing in the Twin Cities to the Oromo Relief Association of North America, founded in 1981 to help refugees and find sponsor families. The list below includes Orthodox, evangelical and Muslim congregations, sports federations, a political advocacy group and a relief fund, and no one group speaks for all. We did not find a current Minnesota association for Tigrayan, Gurage or Anuak people, or a non-Oromo Ethiopian Muslim association. That is a limit of what we found, and staff can ask. The list below is not complete, and listing here says nothing about who a person trusts.

entries.type: Government (foreign consulate), not a community nonprofit

entries.name: Ethiopian Sports Federation in North America
entries.location: National; the tournament moves between cities
entries.purpose: A nonprofit with an unpaid board that has run an annual soccer tournament and cultural festival since 1984. Its 43rd tournament, with 32 teams and more than 20,000 people expected, was held in the Twin Cities from June 27 to July 4, 2026, with most games at TCO Stadium in Eagan and some at Saint Thomas Academy, and the governor declared July 3 Ethiopian Day. Organizers told MPR News the event nearly left Minnesota because of federal immigration enforcement.

entries.location: Arlington, Virginia, with branch offices and affiliates

entries.name: American Ethiopian Public Affairs Committee
entries.purpose: Promotes U.S.–Ethiopia relations, with voter registration, state chapters and a youth group. Its site listed a September 2026 webinar on violence against Christians in Ethiopia. It is one political voice and does not speak for everyone.

entries.purpose: Started in 2018 by young Tigrayan professionals in the diaspora. Provides relief and development aid in Tigray, with more urgency after November 2020. It lists a Tigray Community of Minnesota among its partners, though we could not reach a website for that group.

entries.purpose: Serves the Orthodox church through education, youth formation, social aid and Amharic religious programming. Its site was posting in October 2026 and does not mention Minnesota.
